title: Cybersecurity CEO Indicted for Allegedly Scamming Millions From Ransomware Victims
author: Renee Dudley
content:
A Florida man who was the subject of a 2019 investigation by ProPublica [was
indicted last month](https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/owner-florida-
ransomware-remediation-company-charged-defrauding-clients) on federal charges
that he defrauded clients of his ransomware data recovery firm.

According to the Justice Department, the man, Zohar Pinhasi, told customers he
could recover their encrypted files without having to pay hackers, when, in
reality, he paid the ransom and charged victims a hefty fee on top.

The indictment mirrors the findings from ProPublica’s 2019 article “[The Trade
Secret](https://features.propublica.org/ransomware/ransomware-attack-data-
recovery-firms-paying-hackers/),” which centered on Pinhasi and his scheme.
The outlet found that the ransomware victims were being harmed twice: once by
the hackers, who locked their targets’ files and demanded ransom, and a second
time by MonsterCloud, Pinhasi’s Florida-based data recovery firm, which misled
its clients about not paying ransoms.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2019/05/20190515-ransomware-3x2.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **The
Trade Secret: Firms That Promised High-Tech Ransomware Solutions Almost Always
Just Pay the Hackers**
](https://features.propublica.org/ransomware/ransomware-attack-data-recovery-
firms-paying-hackers/)

“By falsely claiming to decrypt ransomware without paying off the ransomers,
the defendant re-victimized his clients while extracting a hefty profit for
himself,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in an Oct. 7 press release. “Our
Office will vigorously prosecute ransomware attackers who prey on Americans
from across the world and those who cynically profit from their criminal
activity.”

When ProPublica published its story in 2019, ransomware was growing into one
of the world’s most pervasive cyberthreats. Hackers locked the data of
governments, schools and businesses, holding the decryption key for a ransom
payment, which they usually demanded in bitcoin and other types of difficult-
to-trace cryptocurrency.

ProPublica’s reporting focused on how U.S. industries, from data recovery
firms like MonsterCloud to [insurance
giants](https://www.propublica.org/article/the-extortion-economy-how-
insurance-companies-are-fueling-a-rise-in-ransomware-attacks) that cover
ransom payments, all fueled the [extortion
economy](https://www.propublica.org/series/ransomware-enablers). Ransomware
remains a widespread threat today, and the threat to national security has
grown as hackers linked to hostile foreign governments are believed to [use
ransomware](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2023/jul/17/ransomware-
gangs-companies-cyber-crime-hackers) as a cover for espionage. The prevalence
of AI tools is also making it [easier](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ai-linked-
ransomeware-attacks-global-cybersecurity-report/) for attackers to spread
ransomware.

Pinhasi, who went by the alias Zack Green, told ProPublica in 2019 that
MonsterCloud never promised clients that their data will be recovered by any
particular method. “How we do it, it’s our problem,” he told ProPublica. “You
will get your data back. Sit back, relax and enjoy the ride.” He called
MonsterCloud’s data recovery methods a “trade secret.”

Pinhasi hung up when reached on his cellphone this month. A message left with
a representative at MonsterCloud’s office phone number and a message left with
his attorney were not returned. A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office
said Pinhasi pleaded not guilty to the federal charges.

In its 2019 investigation, ProPublica interviewed MonsterCloud’s clients and
ransomware experts and found that in certain cases the firm must have paid
ransoms on behalf of clients. MonsterCloud’s services were particularly
popular with local law enforcement agencies, who are loath to engage with or
pay criminal hackers. Several interviewed by ProPublica at the time said they
chose MonsterCloud to help them recover from ransomware because they believed
the firm would never pay a ransom.

Pinhasi, who described himself to ProPublica as a former IT security
intelligence officer for the Israeli military, said in 2019 that MonsterCloud
handled up to 30 calls a day and had about 20 employees in South Florida as
well as extensive global contacts.

Federal investigators found that, over the course of the scheme, Pinhasi
allegedly charged clients more than $19 million and paid more than $8 million
in ransom payments. In one example, Pinhasi made a ransom payment of about
$8,200 but charged the client about $150,000. If convicted, he faces up to 20
years in prison.

In the Justice Department’s October press release, an FBI official said
Pinhasi had “turned the victim’s crisis into his own profit center. This
deception is unacceptable, and the FBI is committed to ensuring accountability
for those who choose to victimize the very people who trusted them for help.”

The Justice Department did not address ProPublica’s 2019 finding that one of
the FBI’s own was among Pinhasi’s associates at MonsterCloud. John Pistole, a
former deputy director of the FBI under Robert Mueller, was prominently
featured in a promotional video on MonsterCloud’s homepage. “Police
departments, government agencies, hospitals, small business and Fortune 500
firms trust MonsterCloud to help recover from attacks and protect against new
ones,” Pistole said in the video. “MonsterCloud’s proprietary technology and
expertise protects their professional reputations and organizational
integrity.”

Pistole was not mentioned by name in the Pinhasi indictment.

In 2019, Pinhasi touted MonsterCloud’s ties to law enforcement as evidence of
its integrity. Pistole, who also headed the Transportation Security
Administration under President Barack Obama, was listed on MonsterCloud’s
website as the only member of its “Cyber Security Advisory Council.”

Pistole did not respond to a request for comment for this story. In a 2019
interview, he said he became acquainted with Pinhasi after MonsterCloud
reached him through a speaker’s bureau and that MonsterCloud paid him
indirectly through that group. He said Pinhasi scripted his testimonial and
that he was well aware that in most cases — including MonsterCloud’s — the
only way to decrypt data locked by ransomware is to pay the hackers. “That’s
the business model as I understood it,” Pistole told ProPublica at the time.
“Based on my experience and knowledge, ransom is paid and they facilitate the
best practices moving forward.”

A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on Pistole’s
connection to MonsterCloud.
